examples: My sister has really nice skin.
In winter my skin is dry.
I got sun so my skin is red.
nuance: 피부 means the skin of the body and is often praised when it looks clear and healthy. To say skin is dry use 건조하다, and Koreans care a lot about keeping the 피부 smooth.
mistakes: Saying 피부가 말라요 instead of 피부가 건조해요

examples: I fell and broke a bone.
If I drink milk my bones are strong.
I am getting old so my bones are weak.
nuance: 뼈 means a bone inside the body and is used to talk about breaks and strength. For a broken bone Koreans say 뼈가 부러지다 with 부러지다, the verb for snapping hard things.
mistakes: Saying 뼈가 깨졌어요 instead of 뼈가 부러졌어요

examples: I worked out a lot so my muscles hurt.
That person has a lot of muscle.
I sat long so my muscle is knotted.
nuance: 근육 means muscle and often hurts after exercise or hard work. For a stiff knotted muscle Koreans say 근육이 뭉치다 with 뭉치다, a special verb for clumping up.
mistakes: Saying 근육이 딱딱해요 instead of 근육이 뭉쳤어요

examples: I exercised so my heart beats fast.
I was surprised so my heart races.
My grandfather has a weak heart.
nuance: 심장 means the physical heart organ that beats inside the chest. For emotions Koreans use 마음 or 가슴 instead, so 심장 stays mostly medical or physical.
mistakes: Using 심장 for feelings when 마음 is needed

examples: I get a blood test at the hospital.
nuance: 혈액 is the formal medical word for blood used in hospitals and tests. In daily talk about bleeding from a cut Koreans usually say 피, so 혈액 sounds clinical.
mistakes: Using 혈액 for a bleeding cut instead of 피

examples: You must not spit on the street.
My throat hurts so swallowing is hard.
My mouth waters at the tasty smell.
nuance: 침 means the saliva inside your mouth and is used with verbs like spit and swallow. Note that 침 is also the word for an acupuncture needle, so context decides the meaning.
mistakes: Confusing 침 saliva with 침 the acupuncture needle

examples: I exercise so I sweat a lot.
It is hot so I sweat.
I wipe the sweat with a towel.
nuance: 땀 means sweat and pairs with 흘리다 to say someone is sweating a lot. The phrase 땀이 나다 is the everyday way to say sweat appears when it is hot.
mistakes: Saying 땀을 해요 instead of 땀을 흘려요 or 땀이 나요

examples: I watched a sad movie so tears come.
I wipe my tears with my hand.
I yawned so tears came out.
nuance: 눈물 means tears and most naturally pairs with 나다 to say tears come out. Saying someone has a lot of 눈물 means they cry easily, not that they make much liquid.
mistakes: Saying 눈물을 울어요 instead of 눈물이 나요

examples: I climbed stairs so I am out of breath.
nuance: 숨 means a breath and uses 쉬다 to mean breathe, the same verb that also means rest. To say you are out of breath Koreans say 숨이 차다 with the verb 차다.
mistakes: Saying 숨을 해요 instead of 숨을 쉬어요

usage: there is a lot of beard
examples: My grandfather has a long beard.
Dad shaves his beard in the morning.
These days I am growing a beard.
nuance: 수염 covers both the beard and the mustache, so context shows which one. To shave it Koreans use 깎다, the same verb as for cutting hair short, not 자르다.
mistakes: Saying 수염을 잘라요 instead of 수염을 깎아요

examples: The wrinkles around my eyes are deep.
nuance: 주름 means a wrinkle on the skin and also a fold or crease in cloth. For new wrinkles forming Koreans say 주름이 생기다 with 생기다, the verb for something coming into being.
mistakes: Saying 주름이 나요 instead of 주름이 생겼어요

examples: I have one mole on my face.
I remove the mole at a clinic.
A mole appeared on my back.
nuance: 점 means a mole on the skin and also a dot or point in other contexts. To remove a mole Koreans use 빼다, the verb for taking out, not 지우다 which is for erasing.
mistakes: Saying 점을 지워요 instead of 점을 빼요
